comparison: Both evaluate behavioral findings showing odor-specific serotonin effects (C2, C26-C28). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers consistently acknowledge these findings as interesting observations, with all three reviewers recognizing the odor-specificity. Strong agreement on support for these behavioral claims.

OpenEval evaluates dose-response relationships (C29-C33) as supported. Peer review R1 partially overlaps (C31-C33) as part of broader behavioral findings. Both find the concentration-dependent effects well-documented, though peer review groups these with other behavioral data rather than treating dose-response as a separate evaluation.

Both address spontaneous firing changes in PNs (C34-C38). OpenEval finds ISI analysis and firing pattern changes well-supported with strong statistics. Peer reviewers accept these findings, with Reviewer 1 noting serotonin 'induces spontaneous bursting in PNs' and Reviewer 2 acknowledging 'baseline firing' increases. Strong agreement on support.

Perfect claim overlap (C39-C41) on current injection experiments showing altered PN excitability. OpenEval notes support but flags small sample size (n=4). Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge, treating them as supporting evidence for excitability changes. Both find the data supportive despite OpenEval's caveat about sample size.

Both evaluate odor-evoked response enhancement (C3, C48-C51). OpenEval finds systematic evidence across 82 PN-odor combinations well-supported. Peer reviewers accept the uniform enhancement of PN responses, with Reviewer 2 noting PNs 'generally increase their odor responses.' Agreement on the basic finding of enhanced responses.

Partial overlap on temporal feature preservation (C44-C46, C52). OpenEval finds preservation of temporal features well-demonstrated. Peer review R3 raises concern that differential effects across odors at the physiological level were not shown, suggesting evidence for preserved combinatorial coding may be incomplete. Divergence in confidence level.

Both address preserved odor identity and combinatorial coding (C4-C5, C54, C56-C58). OpenEval finds PCA and correlation analyses demonstrate preservation. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer 2 noting authors 'do not show if PN responses to different odors were differently affected.' OpenEval more confident than peer reviewers about completeness of evidence.

Strong overlap on linear model claims (C7, C60-C61, C65-C71). OpenEval finds model predictions and mechanistic framework well-supported with good generalization. Peer reviewers express significant uncertainty about generalizability and causal interpretation, questioning whether model works for overlapping PN representations and noting 'theoretical discrepancy between physiology and behavior.' Major divergence in evaluation.

Perfect claim overlap (C72-C77) on fed vs hungry locust experiments. OpenEval finds data supported and appropriately acknowledges non-specificity (C77). Peer reviewers uncertain, stating authors 'did not fully tone down their claims regarding causality' and noting 'no proof that serotonin injection mimics starved behavioral responses.' Disagreement on whether caveats are sufficiently emphasized.

Perfect claim overlap (C85-C86) on neural ensemble segregation. OpenEval finds extracellular data supports distinct ensembles and early segregation. Peer reviewers uncertain about generalizability, questioning whether findings hold for odors with overlapping PN activation beyond the three tested odors. Divergence on strength of conclusion.

Perfect claim overlap (C6, C82) on interpretive conclusion about enhanced sensitivity with preserved identity. OpenEval finds interpretation well-supported by combined findings. Peer reviewers accept this basic interpretation, with editor noting work shows 'odorant-specific effects despite similar consequences on all projection neuronal types.' Agreement on this high-level interpretation.

Both address temporal stability of serotonin effects (C100-C101). OpenEval finds Figure supplement data supports temporal stability. Peer Reviewer 1 raises significant concern about linking 5-10 minute physiological effects to 3-hour behavioral effects, noting this timing difference as a 'caveat.' Divergence: OpenEval accepts temporal stability data, peer reviewer questions physiological-behavioral linkage across time.

Minimal overlap (C100) on experimental timing methods. OpenEval evaluates methods as appropriately detailed. Peer review R7 questions the different timing for physiology (5-10 min) vs behavior (3 hr), treating this as a methodological concern rather than accepting the methods description. Different focus: OpenEval on completeness, peer on validity.

OpenEval evaluates PN identification methods (C107-C108) as supported by established properties and visual confirmation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing cell identification validation.

OpenEval evaluates odorant characterization claims (C20-C22, C94) as supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing odorant selection justification.

OpenEval evaluates speculative claim about compensatory mechanisms (C80) as appropriately uncertain with no direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific hypothesis.

OpenEval evaluates literature context claims (C1, C8-C19, C78, C83, C87, C90) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically assessing citation appropriateness for background claims.

OpenEval evaluates citations for linear model framework (C63-C64) as appropriate for contextualizing the modeling approach. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific citations.

OpenEval evaluates interpretive claims about contradictions and neural-behavioral links (C79, C81) as reasonable. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these interpretive statements.

OpenEval evaluates general statement about segregation locations (C84) as appropriately qualified and conceptually sound. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this contextual claim.
